_comment: Measured quality floors. A change that drops below any of these fails the guard.
These are FLOORS, not targets. Raise them when a change earns it, deliberately,
in the same commit that earns it. Lowering one is a decision that must be argued
in a commit message, never a convenience to make a build pass.
THE HELD-OUT SPLIT CHANGED, so numbers before 2026-09-01 are NOT comparable.
mechanism/appliesTo used to be held out and are now indexed; observation notes
and prediction reasoning replaced them. See src/lib/cairn/evalset.ts. The old
split scored 0.895 and the new one scores 0.836 on the same retriever -- the
new split is harder because it is people describing an encounter in their own
words rather than the author's own explanation of the finding.
Two suites are tracked because they measure different query distributions and
have disagreed. Held-out queries are plentiful; agent queries are real tool
stderr, representative but few. A change that improves one and damages the
other is a trade to be made consciously, which is why both appear here.

heldOut._source: npm run cairn:eval — observation notes and prediction reasoning, never indexed
_note: REBASED. The former split (mechanism/appliesTo) is now indexed and appears in
the report as an in-sample tripwire scoring 1.000, which measures nothing.
Indexing those fields was measured on THIS split, held out both before and
after, which is the only comparison that means anything:
before  P@1 0.821  P@5 0.910  MRR 0.864  delivery 0.851
after   P@1 0.836  P@5 0.910  MRR 0.876  delivery 0.851
One case of 67. Worth having and far short of what the old split implied,
for the reason recorded in evalset.ts: a field cannot be indexed and held
out, so 1.000 on the old split was the measurement collapsing, not accuracy.
The weak-field damp is a real trade and was chosen on the machine suite.
At damp >= 0.8 held-out is 0.851 and machine stderr drops to 7/8; at <= 0.7
held-out is 0.836, P@5 is better (0.910 vs 0.896) and machine holds 8/8.
Machine stderr is what production actually receives, so it wins.
LOWERED 0.86 -> 0.84 and MRR 0.87 -> 0.88 on 2026-09-01 when cairn-0032 was
added. A new finding competes with the existing ones, so P@1 moving is
expected and is not a regression in the ranker: 0.864 -> 0.851 is one case
of 67. The floor moves because the corpus changed, which is the one reason
it is allowed to.
LOWERED AGAIN 0.84 -> 0.83 (MRR 0.88 -> 0.87, delivery 0.86 -> 0.85) on
2026-09-01 when cairn-0033 was added: 0.851 -> 0.838 over 68 cases.
That is the SECOND time these floors have been argued down for the same
reason, and the argument was true both times. It is also exactly what a
genuine ranker regression would look like in a commit message, which is why
an aggregate floor cannot be the last line of defence. It is now the second
line. data/case-outcomes.json records the outcome of every held-out case
individually and cairn:case-guard reports the set difference, so a corpus
that grew and a ranker that broke stop being the same number.
Measured, not asserted: adding cairn-0033 broke zero existing cases -- the
whole 0.013 drop is its own first case failing, against a denominator one
larger. Dropping EXPLAINED_WEIGHT 1.0 -> 0.85 costs a comparable amount of
P@1 and DOES break an existing case (cairn-0019). Identical movement in the
average, opposite meanings, and only the per-case check can tell them apart.
RRF's k moved 60 -> 2 on 2026-09-01, and it is the first threshold in this
project chosen against more than a handful of cases. k=60 is the value from
the original RRF work, which fused TREC runs of about a thousand documents.
On a corpus of forty it inverts its own intent: 1/(60+1) against 1/(60+2) is
a 1.6% gap, so every ranker contributes nearly the same amount however
decisively it ranks, and the fusion averages noise.
Found by the agent suite, not by these numbers. On the proxy 403 stderr,
cairn-0001 led THREE of four rankers and lost the fusion by 0.16%.
Swept 1..7 and 15/30/60 on two corpora (69 and 71 held-out cases). P@1,
delivery and the agent suite are flat across the entire range; P@5 and the
proxy case are not, and the cliff sits between 3 and 4 on BOTH corpora --
a property of the ranking structure rather than of corpus size. 2 is the
paper's own ratio rescaled to these list lengths (k ~ N/17, N ~ 37) and sits
mid-plateau with two steps of headroom.
P@5 IS THIN: 0.901 against a floor of 0.90, one case from red. It was 0.913
before this change on the 69-case corpus and 0.927 after, so the fix improved
it; the two findings admitted alongside cost it again. Worth watching rather
than worth moving.

agent._source: npm run cairn:agent-eval — real commands, real stderr
_note: silentOnUnknown counts 'returned nothing' OR 'returned only weak-labelled
matches' -- both safe; only a confident wrong answer is not.
3/3 since the failing command became evidence. Six statistical methods could
not get the third; the program name that produced the error got all three,
because it is a different KIND of evidence rather than a better weighting of
the same one.

corpus._source: npm run cairn:lint and npm run cairn:doctor

maxFalseWeak._source: fraction of CORRECT answers labelled weak
maxFalseWeak._note: If this climbs the label becomes noise and agents will ignore it.
